statement: Let $X$ be a nonempty [chain-complete poset](c:chain-complete-poset) and let $f\colon X\to X$ be an [inflationary map](c:inflationary-map), so $x\le f(x)$ for every $x$. Then $f$ has a [fixed point](c:fixed-point).

hypotheses.text: The poset $X$ is nonempty.
Every nonempty [chain](c:chain) in $X$ has a [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) in $X$.
The map $f$ satisfies $x\le f(x)$ for all $x\in X$.

conclusion: There is a point $y\in X$ with $f(y)=y$.

proofs.name: Smallest admissible set
proofs.slogan: Build the smallest set closed under $f$ and chain suprema, show that it is a chain, and take its supremum.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The hypothesis $X\neq\emptyset$ only supplies a base point $x_0$; the other steps need no further choice.

roles.why: A nonempty poset gives the base point $x_0$ of the construction.
Chain suprema define the closure condition and give the final supremum.
Inflation makes $[x_0,\infty)$ admissible and orders $y$ against $f(y)$.

steps.slogan: Intersect all admissible sets to get the smallest admissible set $B$.
steps.detail: Fix $x_0\in X$. Call $A\subseteq X$ admissible if $x_0$ is its least element, $f(A)\subseteq A$, and every nonempty [chain](c:chain) inside $A$ has its [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) in $A$. The ray $[x_0,\infty)$ is admissible because $f$ is inflationary, and intersections of admissible sets are admissible, so the intersection $B$ of all of them is the smallest one.

steps.slogan: Split $B$ at an extreme point $y$ into elements below $y$ and elements above $f(y)$.
steps.detail: Call $y\in B$ extreme if $f(z)\le y$ for every $z\in B$ with $z<y$. For extreme $y$, the set of $z\in B$ with $z\le y$ or $f(y)\le z$ is admissible: it is closed under $f$ by the extreme property and inflation, and under chain suprema because a chain either stays below $y$ or has a member above $f(y)$. So this set equals $B$.

steps.slogan: Prove that every element of $B$ is extreme.
steps.detail: The extreme points form an admissible set: $x_0$ is extreme, $f(y)$ is extreme when $y$ is, by the split at $y$, and the supremum of a chain of extreme points is extreme by the split at a chain member. Hence all of $B$ is extreme.

steps.slogan: Show that $B$ is a [chain](c:chain).
steps.detail: Let $y,z\in B$. Because $y$ is extreme, $z\le y$ or $f(y)\le z$, and in the second case $y\le f(y)\le z$ since $f$ is inflationary. So $y$ and $z$ are comparable.

steps.slogan: Take the supremum $y$ of $B$ and show that $f(y)=y$.
steps.detail: The set $B$ is a nonempty chain, so it has a [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound) $y$, and $y\in B$ because $B$ is admissible. Then $f(y)\in B$, so $f(y)\le y$. Inflation gives $y\le f(y)$, hence $f(y)=y$.

concepts.c:chain-complete-poset: The theorem is stated for this kind of order.
concepts.c:inflationary-map: Inflation drives every step of the order comparisons.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The conclusion is the existence of a fixed point.
concepts.c:chain: The smallest admissible set turns out to be a chain.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: The supremum of the chain $B$ is the fixed point.

source.note: mathlib builds the smallest admissible set (bot, bot_isAdmissible), its extreme points (IsExtremePt, bot_eq_of_le_or_map_le), shows that it is a chain (bot_isChain) and takes its cSup; the route is Lang's Algebra.

statement: Let $X$ be a [second-countable space](c:second-countable-space) and $C\subseteq X$ a [closed set](c:closed-set). Then $C=V\cup D$ with $V$ [countable](c:countable-set) and $D$ a [perfect set](c:perfect).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [second-countable](c:second-countable-space).
The set $C\subseteq X$ is [closed](c:closed-set).

conclusion: There are a countable set $V$ and a [perfect](c:perfect) set $D$ with $C=V\cup D$.

proofs.name: Countable basis
proofs.slogan: Remove from $C$ every point that has a neighborhood meeting $C$ in a countable set; what remains is perfect.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A perfect set means closed with no isolated points; $D$ may be empty, and then $C=V$ is countable.

roles.why: A countable basis makes $V\cap C$ a countable union of countable sets.
Closedness of $C$ makes the remainder $D$ closed.

steps.slogan: Collect the basic open sets that meet $C$ in a countable set.
steps.detail: Fix a countable [basis](c:is-topological-basis) $\mathcal B$ of $X$. Let $V$ be the union of all $U\in\mathcal B$ with $U\cap C$ countable, and let $D=C\setminus V$.

steps.slogan: Show that the part $V\cap C$ is countable.
steps.detail: The set $V\cap C$ is the union of the sets $U\cap C$ over the chosen $U\in\mathcal B$. This is a countable union of [countable sets](c:countable-set), so it is countable.

steps.slogan: Show that $D$ is closed in $X$.
steps.detail: The set $V$ is a union of [open sets](c:open-set), so it is open. Hence $D=C\cap(X\setminus V)$ is an intersection of two closed sets, so it is closed.

steps.slogan: Show that no point of $D$ is isolated in $D$.
steps.detail: Let $x\in D$ and let $E$ be a neighborhood of $x$ with $E\cap D$ countable, and pick $U\in\mathcal B$ with $x\in U\subseteq E$. Then $U\cap C\subseteq(E\cap D)\cup(V\cap C)$ is countable, so $U\subseteq V$ and $x\in V$, a contradiction. So every neighborhood of $x$ meets $D$ in an uncountable set, hence in a point other than $x$.

steps.slogan: Write $C$ as the union of $V\cap C$ and $D$.
steps.detail: Since $D=C\setminus V$, we have $C=(V\cap C)\cup D$. The set $V\cap C$ is countable, and $D$ is closed without isolated points, so $D$ is [perfect](c:perfect).

concepts.c:second-countable-space: A countable basis exists and makes the bad set countable.
concepts.c:closed-set: Closedness of $C$ and of $D$ is part of perfectness.
concepts.c:countable-set: The removed part is a countable union of countable sets.
concepts.c:perfect: The remainder $D$ is closed with no isolated points.
concepts.c:is-topological-basis: Basic open sets decide which points to remove.
concepts.c:open-set: The removed set $V$ is open, so $D$ is closed.

source.note: mathlib takes a countable basis (TopologicalSpace.exists_countable_basis), V the union of basic sets with countable trace on C, D = C \ V, and proves Perfect D with preperfect_iff_nhds and Countable.biUnion.

statement: Let $(X,\mu)$ be a [measure space](c:measure-space), $f\colon X\to[0,\infty)$ [measurable](c:measurable-function), and $g\ge0$ measurable and integrable on each $[0,t]$, with $G(s)=\int_0^s g$. Then $\int_X G(f)\,d\mu=\int_0^\infty g(t)\,\mu\{f\ge t\}\,dt$ in $[0,\infty]$.

hypotheses.text: $(X,\mu)$ is a [measure space](c:measure-space).
The function $f\colon X\to[0,\infty)$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function).
The weight $g\colon[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ is measurable and integrable on every interval $[0,t]$.

conclusion: The [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) of $G(f)$ equals $\int_0^\infty g(t)\,\mu\{f\ge t\}\,dt$, which integrates $g$ against the tail form $t\mapsto\mu\{f\ge t\}$ of the [distribution function](c:distribution-function) of $f$.

formal.difference: The declaration needs only almost everywhere measurability and non-negativity of $f$, and almost everywhere non-negativity of $g$ on $(0,\infty)$. Changing $f$ or $g$ on a null set changes neither side, so the statements agree.

proofs.name: Tonelli on the region under the graph
proofs.slogan: Write $G(f)$ as an integral over $t$, swap the two integrals by Tonelli, and read off the slice measure.
proofs.scope: The layer-cake form with both sides possibly infinite; the case $g=1$ gives $\int f\,d\mu=\int_0^\infty\mu\{f\ge t\}\,dt$, the slice form of Cavalieri's principle. A case split reduces the proof to a sigma-finite measure.

roles.why: Tonelli needs a sigma-finite measure, so the proof reduces the space to that case.
Measurability of $f$ makes the region under its graph a measurable set.
Non-negativity of $g$ gives the Lebesgue integral form and justifies Tonelli.

steps.slogan: Write $G(f(\omega))$ as the integral of $g(t)\,\mathbf 1_{\{t\le f(\omega)\}}$ over $t>0$.
steps.detail: Because $g\ge0$, $G(f(\omega))=\int_0^{f(\omega)}g=\int_{(0,\infty)}g(t)\,\mathbf 1_{\{t\le f(\omega)\}}\,dt$ as a [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) with value in $[0,\infty]$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to a [sigma-finite](c:sigma-finite-measure) measure by cutting off the region where $g$ vanishes.
steps.detail: If $g=0$ almost everywhere, both sides vanish; if some $s>0$ has $\int_0^s g>0$ and $\mu\{f>s\}=\infty$, both sides are infinite. Otherwise let $M$ be the largest number with $g=0$ a.e. on $(0,M]$: then $\mu$ restricted to $\{f>M\}$ is sigma-finite, and points with $f\le M$ add nothing to either side.

steps.slogan: Swap the integrals over $\omega$ and $t$ by Tonelli's theorem.
steps.detail: The set $\{(\omega,t):0<t\le f(\omega)\}$ is measurable in $X\times(0,\infty)$ because $f$ is measurable. So the integrand $g(t)\,\mathbf 1_{\{t\le f(\omega)\}}$ is non-negative and product-measurable. Tonelli's theorem for the sigma-finite measure $\mu$ and Lebesgue measure lets us integrate over $\omega$ first.

steps.slogan: Compute the inner integral over $\omega$ as the tail measure $\mu\{f\ge t\}$.
steps.detail: For fixed $t>0$, $\int_X\mathbf 1_{\{t\le f(\omega)\}}\,d\mu=\mu\{f\ge t\}$, the tail form of the [distribution function](c:distribution-function) of $f$. So the iterated integral is $\int_0^\infty g(t)\,\mu\{f\ge t\}\,dt$, the right side.

concepts.c:measure-space: The proof integrates over a general measure space.
concepts.c:measurable-function: Measurability of $f$ makes the level sets and the product region measurable.
concepts.c:lebesgue-integral: Both sides are Lebesgue integrals with values in $[0,\infty]$.
concepts.c:distribution-function: The tail measure $\mu\{f\ge t\}$ is the weight that remains after the swap.

source.note: mathlib replaces f and g by measurable versions, reduces to sigma-finite measures (lintegral_comp_eq_lintegral_meas_le_mul_of_measurable) and swaps the integrals with lintegral_lintegral_swap.

statement: Every [simple](c:simple-group) [finite group](c:finite-group) is isomorphic to a [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) of prime order, an [alternating group](c:alternating-group) $A_n$ with $n\ge5$, a [group of Lie type](c:group-of-lie-type) (the Tits group included), or one of 26 [sporadic groups](c:sporadic-finite-simple-group).

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group) that is [simple](c:simple-group).

conclusion: $G$ is isomorphic to a group on this list, and two groups on the list are isomorphic only through known isomorphisms such as $A_5\cong\mathrm{PSL}_2(5)$.

proofs.name: Minimal counterexample outline
proofs.slogan: Take a minimal counterexample, split it by the type of its 2-local subgroups, and identify it with a listed group, a contradiction.
proofs.scope: An outline of the whole classification, not a complete proof: each step rests on the cited volumes. The simplicity of the listed groups, which shows that they occur, is classical and is not reproved.

roles.why: Finiteness gives Sylow methods and a minimal counterexample; simplicity forces local analysis.

steps.slogan: Assume a counterexample of least order, all of whose proper simple sections are listed.
steps.detail: Let $G$ be a simple group of least order that is not on the list. Every simple section of a proper subgroup is then listed, and the Feit-Thompson theorem shows that $G$ has even order. So a [Sylow](c:sylow-subgroup) 2-subgroup is nontrivial and $G$ has an [involution](c:involution).

steps.slogan: Split the counterexample by the structure of its 2-local subgroups.
steps.detail: The published proof separates groups of characteristic 2 type, in which every 2-local subgroup $H$ has $F^*(H)=O_2(H)$, from all other groups. The other groups are treated through centralizers of involutions and signalizer functors, and the two cases use different methods.

steps.slogan: Remove the small and very rigid cases by uniqueness theorems.
steps.detail: Uniqueness theorems, of the kind of Bender's theorem on strongly embedded subgroups, identify $G$ whenever a 2-local subgroup is unusually large or $G$ has a strongly embedded subgroup. The Gorenstein-Lyons-Solomon volume on uniqueness theorems proves them in the form that the later steps need.

steps.slogan: Identify the groups of characteristic 2 type with listed groups.
steps.detail: For characteristic 2 type, the trichotomy and uniqueness theorems together with the treatment of quasithin groups show that $G$ is a [group of Lie type](c:group-of-lie-type) in characteristic 2 or another listed group. Aschbacher, Lyons, Smith and Solomon carry this out in the characteristic 2 volume.

steps.slogan: Identify the remaining groups through components and signalizer functors.
steps.detail: For the other groups, signalizer functor methods produce a component in an involution centralizer, and classification of groups with a given standard component identifies $G$. Gorenstein, Lyons and Solomon treat the generic case and the special odd case in Numbers 5 and 6.

steps.slogan: Conclude that every case gives a listed group and that the list has no further repeats.
steps.detail: Each case ends with $G$ isomorphic to a listed group, which contradicts the choice of $G$. Conversely every listed group is simple, and the isomorphisms among them are the known small coincidences, so the list is complete and repeats a group only through those.

concepts.c:simple-group: The theorem classifies simple groups, and the counterexample is one.
concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness gives Sylow theory and a minimal counterexample.
concepts.c:cyclic-group: The cyclic groups of prime order are the abelian simple groups.
concepts.c:alternating-group: The alternating groups $A_n$ with $n\ge5$ form one family on the list.
concepts.c:group-of-lie-type: Groups of Lie type form the main infinite family on the list.
concepts.c:sporadic-finite-simple-group: The 26 sporadic groups are the exceptions on the list.
concepts.c:involution: Centralizers of involutions drive the identification of the group.

source.ref: D. Gorenstein, R. Lyons and R. Solomon, The Classification of the Finite Simple Groups, Numbers 1-6, Mathematical Surveys and Monographs 40, American Mathematical Society, 1994-2005; with M. Aschbacher, R. Lyons, S. D. Smith and R. Solomon, The Classification of Finite Simple Groups: Groups of Characteristic 2 Type, Mathematical Surveys and Monographs 172, American Mathematical Society, 2011
source.note: The steps follow the minimal counterexample strategy of the second-generation proof; the url is the page of Number 5 of the series.

statement: Let $C$ be a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) with [associator](c:associator) $\alpha$ and unit isomorphisms $\lambda,\rho$ that satisfy the pentagon and triangle identities. Then any two composites of instances of $\alpha$, $\lambda$, $\rho$ and their inverses, built with $\otimes$ and identities, that join the same two bracketed words are equal.

hypotheses.text: $C$ is a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category): $\otimes$ is a bifunctor with unit $I$, and $\alpha,\lambda,\rho$ are [natural isomorphisms](c:natural-isomorphism).
The associator satisfies the [pentagon identity](c:pentagon-identity).
The associator and the unit isomorphisms satisfy the triangle identity.

conclusion: Every diagram of structural isomorphisms between bracketed words commutes.

proofs.name: Normal forms of bracketed words
proofs.slogan: Send every bracketed word to its right-bracketed normal form by a canonical arrow, and show that every structural arrow respects it.
proofs.scope: Mac Lane's coherence theorem for monoidal categories, as an outline of the published proof. The proof works with formal arrows between words in letters, and evaluation in $C$ then transfers the equalities.

roles.why: Naturality lets a structural arrow slide out of a tensor context, and evaluation preserves equalities.
The pentagon proves that two ways to rebracket a triple of normal forms agree.
The triangle, with the pentagon, handles the unit letters, including $\lambda_I=\rho_I$.

steps.slogan: Replace the claim by one about formal arrows between words in letters.
steps.detail: Words are built from letters and the unit by $\otimes$, and formal arrows are terms built from $\alpha$, $\lambda$, $\rho$, their inverses, identities, composition and $\otimes$. Evaluating a formal arrow in $C$ uses only structural arrows, so equal formal arrows give equal arrows of $C$.

steps.slogan: Define the normal form of each word and a canonical arrow to it.
steps.detail:
The normal form $\mathrm{nf}(w)$ is the right-bracketed word with the unit letters deleted. By induction on $w$, define $
u_w\colon w	o\mathrm{nf}(w)$ as $
u_{u\otimes v}=a_{u,v}\circ(
u_u\otimes
u_v)$, where $a_{u,v}\colon\mathrm{nf}(u)\otimes\mathrm{nf}(v)	o\mathrm{nf}(u\otimes v)$ is built from $\alpha$, $\lambda$ and $ho$.

steps.slogan: Show that the append arrows $a_{u,v}$ are associative and compatible with units.
steps.detail: The two composites $\mathrm{nf}(u)\otimes\mathrm{nf}(v)\otimes\mathrm{nf}(w)\to\mathrm{nf}(u\otimes v\otimes w)$ agree, by induction on the length of $\mathrm{nf}(u)$ with the [pentagon identity](c:pentagon-identity) in the inductive step. The unit cases follow from the triangle identity, which together with the pentagon gives $\lambda_I=\rho_I$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\nu_{w'}\circ g=\nu_w$ for every elementary arrow $g\colon w\to w'$.
steps.detail: An elementary arrow is an instance of $\alpha$, $\lambda$, $\rho$ or an inverse, placed inside a tensor context. Naturality of these [natural isomorphisms](c:natural-isomorphism) and the definition of $\nu$ move the context out by induction on its depth. The instance itself is then settled by the previous step.

steps.slogan: Deduce that any two parallel formal arrows are equal, and transfer this to $C$.
steps.detail:
A formal arrow $f\colon w	o w'$ is a composite of elementary arrows and their inverses, so $
u_{w'}\circ f=
u_w$. Since $
u_{w'}$ is an isomorphism, $f=
u_{w'}^{-1}\circ
u_w$ depends only on $w$ and $w'$. Evaluation in $C$ gives the theorem.

concepts.c:monoidal-category: The theorem is about the structural isomorphisms of a monoidal category.
concepts.c:associator: The associator is the main structural isomorphism to be rebracketed.
concepts.c:natural-isomorphism: Naturality moves a structural arrow out of its context.
concepts.c:pentagon-identity: The pentagon makes rebracketing of four factors consistent.

source.ref: S. Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician, 2nd edition, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 5, Springer, 1998, Chapter VII, Section 2; see also S. Mac Lane, Natural associativity and commutativity, Rice University Studies 49 (1963), 28-46
source.note: The steps outline the normal-form argument for Mac Lane's coherence theorem; the cited chapter proves the identities behind the append and elementary-arrow steps.

statement: Let $X_n$ and $X$ be random vectors in $\mathbb R^k$. Then $X_n\to X$ in [distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) if and only if $\langle t,X_n\rangle\to\langle t,X\rangle$ in distribution for every $t\in\mathbb R^k$. Hence a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^k$ is determined by the laws of its one-dimensional projections.

hypotheses.text: The maps $X_n$ and $X$ are [random variables](c:random-variable) with values in $\mathbb R^k$, possibly on different probability spaces.

conclusion: Convergence in distribution of $X_n$ is equivalent to convergence in distribution of every projection $\langle t,X_n\rangle$, and the laws of all projections fix the law of $X$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves the equivalence only, for random variables in a finite-dimensional real inner product space. The uniqueness consequence is not part of it.

proofs.name: Characteristic functions
proofs.slogan: Compare the characteristic function of a vector at $t$ with that of its projection at $1$, then apply Levy's continuity theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the equivalence proved first and the uniqueness of the law as a consequence. The dimension $k$ is finite, which is used for Levy's continuity theorem.

roles.why: The vectors give characteristic functions $\varphi_X(t)=\mathbb E\,e^{i\langle t,X\rangle}$ and their projections.

steps.slogan: Write the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of $X$ at $t$ through the projection $\langle t,X\rangle$.
steps.detail: For every random vector $Y$ and $t\in\mathbb R^k$, $\varphi_Y(t)=\mathbb E\,e^{i\langle t,Y\rangle}$ is the characteristic function of the real variable $\langle t,Y\rangle$ evaluated at $1$.

steps.slogan: Push the convergence forward by the continuous map $x\mapsto\langle t,x\rangle$.
steps.detail: If $X_n\to X$ in [distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution), then $\langle t,X_n\rangle\to\langle t,X\rangle$ in distribution for each $t$, because $x\mapsto\langle t,x\rangle$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Convert convergence of every projection into convergence of $\varphi_{X_n}(t)$ for every $t$.
steps.detail: Assume that every projection converges in distribution. The function $x\mapsto e^{ix}$ is bounded and continuous, so $\varphi_{\langle t,X_n\rangle}(1)\to\varphi_{\langle t,X\rangle}(1)$. By the identity step, $\varphi_{X_n}(t)\to\varphi_X(t)$ for all $t$.

steps.slogan: Apply Levy's continuity theorem to the pointwise limit of the characteristic functions.
steps.detail: The limit $\varphi_X$ is the characteristic function of the random vector $X$. Levy's continuity theorem on $\mathbb R^k$ then gives $X_n\to X$ in [distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution).

steps.slogan: Take a constant-law sequence to show that projections determine the law.
steps.detail: Let $X'$ be a vector whose projections have the same laws as those of $X$, and let $X_n$ be copies of $X$. Every projection of $X_n$ converges in distribution to the projection of $X'$, so the previous steps give $X_n\to X'$ in distribution. Limits in distribution are unique, so $X'$ and $X$ have the same law.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions with the uniqueness of the law.
steps.detail: The forward step and the Levy step give the equivalence. The constant-law step gives that a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^k$ is determined by its projections.

concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: The theorem compares convergence in distribution of vectors and of projections.
concepts.c:random-variable: The proof treats the vectors as random variables with laws.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: Characteristic functions turn projections into evaluations at one point.

source.note: mathlib proves the forward direction by the continuous mapping theorem (TendstoInDistribution.continuous_comp) and the converse with of_tendsto_charFun and charFun_map_eq_charFun_map_inner_one.

statement: In the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) over a field $K$, let $ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ be triangles [perspective](c:perspective-triangles) from a point $O$. Then the points $AB\cap A'B'$, $BC\cap B'C'$ and $CA\cap C'A'$ lie on one line. Dually, triangles perspective from a line are perspective from a point.

hypotheses.text: The plane is the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) $\mathbb P^2(K)$ over a field $K$, whose points are the lines of $K^3$ through $0$.
$ABC$ and $A'B'C'$ are [triangles](c:triangle) with non-collinear vertices, corresponding vertices differ, and corresponding sides lie on different lines.
The lines $AA'$, $BB'$ and $CC'$ meet in a point $O$ that is none of the six vertices.

conclusion: The three points $AB\cap A'B'$, $BC\cap B'C'$, $CA\cap C'A'$ are collinear, and the dual statement gives the converse.

proofs.name: Vectors in homogeneous coordinates
proofs.slogan: Choose vector representatives with $o=a+a'=b+b'=c+c'$, so the three differences represent the meeting points and sum to zero.
proofs.scope: The direction from a point to a line over any field; the converse is the same statement in the dual plane, which is $\mathbb P^2(K)$ again. Degenerate positions, such as the center on a vertex, are excluded by the hypotheses.

roles.why: Homogeneous coordinates turn points into vectors of $K^3$ and lines into planes through $0$.
Independence of $a,b$ and distinct sides make each side intersection a single point.
The center lies on each line of corresponding vertices, so $o$ is a combination of $a,a'$.

steps.slogan: Choose vector representatives with $o=a+a'=b+b'=c+c'$.
steps.detail: Let $o,a,a'$ be vectors in $K^3$ representing $O,A,A'$. The points are distinct and collinear, so $o=\alpha a+\alpha'a'$ with $\alpha,\alpha'\ne0$, and rescaling $a$ and $a'$ gives $o=a+a'$. The same argument for $B,B'$ and $C,C'$ gives $o=b+b'=c+c'$ with the same $o$.

steps.slogan: Show that $a-b$ represents the point $AB\cap A'B'$, and likewise for the other sides.
steps.detail: From $a+a'=b+b'$ we get $a-b=b'-a'$. This nonzero vector lies in the span of $a,b$ and in the span of $a',b'$, so it represents a point on both lines $AB$ and $A'B'$, which differ, so that point is $AB\cap A'B'$. In the same way $b-c$ and $c-a$ represent the other two points.

steps.slogan: Show that the three vectors sum to zero, so their points are collinear.
steps.detail: We have $(a-b)+(b-c)+(c-a)=0$. So the three vectors are [linearly dependent](c:linear-independence) and span a subspace of dimension at most $2$ of $K^3$. This is contained in a plane through $0$, that is, a line of $\mathbb P^2(K)$.

steps.slogan: Dualize the statement to obtain the converse.
steps.detail: The duality of $\mathbb P^2(K)$ exchanges points and lines, vertices and sides, center and axis. Applied to the proved direction, it shows that triangles perspective from a line are perspective from a point.

concepts.c:projective-plane: Points and lines of the plane become vectors and planes in $K^3$.
concepts.c:perspective-triangles: The hypothesis and the conclusion are the two kinds of perspectivity.
concepts.c:triangle: Non-degenerate triangles make the side intersections well defined.
concepts.c:linear-independence: A zero sum of three vectors makes them dependent.

source.note: The standard vector proof in homogeneous coordinates; mathlib has no Desargues theorem.

statement: Let $M$ be a structure for a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) language $L$, let $s\subseteq M$, and let $\kappa$ be an infinite [cardinal](c:cardinal-number) with $|s|\le\kappa$, $|L|\le\kappa$ and $\kappa\le|M|$. Then $M$ has an [elementary substructure](c:elementary-substructure) $S$ with $s\subseteq S$ and $|S|=\kappa$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is an $L$-structure for a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) language $L$, and $s\subseteq M$.
The cardinal $\kappa$ is infinite.
The set $s$ has at most $\kappa$ elements.
The language $L$ has at most $\kappa$ symbols.
The cardinal $\kappa$ is at most $|M|$.

conclusion: There is an [elementary substructure](c:elementary-substructure) $S\preceq M$ with $s\subseteq S$ and $|S|=\kappa$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the cardinal bounds with universe lifts, so that $M$, $s$ and $\kappa$ may live in different universes, and it measures $L$ by its number of symbols. Otherwise the statements agree.

proofs.name: Skolem closure
proofs.slogan: Add Skolem functions, close $s$ together with a set of size $\kappa$ under them, and count the closure.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Since $\kappa$ is infinite and $\kappa\le|M|$, the structure $M$ is infinite and in particular nonempty.

roles.why: The structure gives the values of the Skolem functions by choice.
Infinite $\kappa$ makes the count of terms and finite tuples equal to $\kappa$.
The bound $|s|\le\kappa$ keeps $|s\cup s'|=\kappa$.
At most $\kappa$ symbols give at most $\kappa$ Skolem functions.
The bound $\kappa\le|M|$ allows a subset $s'$ of size $\kappa$.

steps.slogan: Add a [Skolem function](c:skolemization) symbol for every formula and interpret it by choice.
steps.detail: For each $L$-formula $\varphi(x,\bar y)$, add a function symbol $f_\varphi$ of arity $|\bar y|$. In $M$, let $f_\varphi(\bar b)$ be an element $a$ with $M\models\varphi(a,\bar b)$ when one exists, and any element otherwise. The expanded language $L^*$ has at most $\max(|L|,\aleph_0)\le\kappa$ symbols, because formulas are finite strings.

steps.slogan: Choose a subset $s'\subseteq M$ of size $\kappa$ and close $s\cup s'$ under the functions of $L^*$.
steps.detail: Since $\kappa\le|M|$, pick $s'\subseteq M$ with $|s'|=\kappa$. Let $S$ be the smallest subset of $M$ that contains $s\cup s'$ and is closed under every function of $L^*$, constants included. Then $S$ is an $L$-substructure of $M$.

steps.slogan: Count the closure to show that $|S|=\kappa$.
steps.detail: Every element of $S$ is the value of an $L^*$-term at a finite tuple from $s\cup s'$. There are at most $\max(|s\cup s'|,|L^*|,\aleph_0)=\kappa$ such pairs, so $|S|\le\kappa$. Also $s'\subseteq S$ gives $|S|\ge\kappa$.

steps.slogan: Check the Tarski-Vaught condition to show that $S$ is an [elementary substructure](c:elementary-substructure) of $M$.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi(x,\bar y)$ be an $L$-formula and $\bar b\in S$ with $M\models\exists x\,\varphi(x,\bar b)$. Then $f_\varphi(\bar b)$ is a witness in $M$, and it lies in $S$ because $S$ is closed under $f_\varphi$. By the Tarski-Vaught test, $S\preceq M$.

steps.slogan: Combine the properties of $S$ with the choice of $s$.
steps.detail: The set $S$ contains $s$ by construction, it is an elementary substructure of $M$ by the Tarski-Vaught check, and it has cardinality $\kappa$ by the count.

concepts.c:first-order-logic: Formulas of the language define the Skolem functions and the elementarity.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: The proof counts terms and tuples to bound the size of $S$.
concepts.c:elementary-substructure: The conclusion asks for a substructure preserving all formulas.
concepts.c:skolemization: Skolem functions witness existential formulas inside the closure.

statement: Let $\mathcal C\subseteq H_1\otimes\cdots\otimes H_n$ be a code of dimension at least $2$ with projector $P$ that detects every error on one factor: $PEP=c(E)P$. Then the [transversal gates](c:transversal-gate) $U_1\otimes\cdots\otimes U_n$ that preserve $\mathcal C$ act on it as a finite group modulo phases, so they are not universal.

hypotheses.text: The code $\mathcal C$ has dimension at least $2$ and sits in a tensor product of finite-dimensional spaces $H_i$.
For every operator $E$ acting on one tensor factor, $PEP=c(E)P$ for a scalar $c(E)$.

conclusion: The logical actions of the transversal gates form a finite group modulo phases, so they are not dense in the logical unitary group.

proofs.name: Lie algebra of the transversal group
proofs.slogan: The transversal gates form a compact Lie group whose identity component acts on the code by phases, so the logical group is finite.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with transversal meaning one unitary per tensor factor and no mixing between factors. Universality fails because a finite subgroup of the projective unitary group of $\mathcal C$ is not dense.

roles.why: Finite dimension makes the unitary groups compact, and dimension at least $2$ makes the logical group infinite.
Detection forces every single-factor generator to act as a scalar on the code.

steps.slogan: Show that the transversal gates preserving $\mathcal C$ form a compact [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$.
steps.detail: Let $K=U(H_1)\times\cdots\times U(H_n)$, a compact Lie group. The condition $U\mathcal C=\mathcal C$ is closed and defines a subgroup $G\subseteq K$. By Cartan's closed subgroup theorem $G$ is a compact Lie group, so its identity component $G_0$ has finite index.

steps.slogan: Write each element of the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) of $G$ as a sum of single-factor terms.
steps.detail: The Lie algebra of $G$ consists of tuples $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ of anti-Hermitian matrices with $e^{t(X_1,\dots,X_n)}\in G$ for all $t$. On $H$ it acts as $\hat X=\sum_iX_i$, each $X_i$ acting on factor $i$ only. Differentiating $e^{t\hat X}\mathcal C=\mathcal C$ gives $\hat X\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal C$.

steps.slogan: Show that each Lie algebra element acts on $\mathcal C$ as a scalar.
steps.detail: Detection gives $PX_iP=\lambda_iP$ for each term. For $v\in\mathcal C$ we get $\hat Xv=P\hat Xv=\sum_i\lambda_i\,v$. So $\hat X$ is the scalar $\lambda=\sum_i\lambda_i$ on $\mathcal C$.

steps.slogan: Show that the identity component acts on $\mathcal C$ by phases.
steps.detail: The group $G_0$ is generated by the exponentials of Lie algebra elements, and $e^{\hat X}$ acts on $\mathcal C$ as the scalar $e^{\lambda}$ with $|e^\lambda|=1$. So every element of $G_0$ acts on $\mathcal C$ as a phase.

steps.slogan: Pass to the finite quotient $G/G_0$ to bound the logical group.
steps.detail: The action of $G$ on $\mathcal C$ modulo phases factors through $G/G_0$, which is finite. A finite subgroup of the projective unitary group of $\mathcal C$ is not dense in it, because that group is infinite when $\dim\mathcal C\ge2$.

concepts.c:transversal-gate: Transversal gates are the gates whose group the proof studies.
concepts.c:lie-group: The transversal group is a compact Lie group with finitely many components.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: Lie algebra elements are sums of single-factor generators that act as scalars.

source.note: After B. Eastin and E. Knill, Restrictions on transversal encoded quantum gate sets, Phys. Rev. Lett. 102, 110502 (2009), arXiv:0811.4262, whose argument goes through the Lie algebra of the transversal group.

statement: Let $(X,\mu)$ be a measure space, $s\subseteq X$ a measurable set of [finite measure](c:finite-measure), and $f_n,g\colon X\to\mathbb R$ [measurable](c:measurable-function) with $f_n\to g$ [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere) on $s$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a measurable $t\subseteq s$ with $\mu(t)\le\varepsilon$ and $f_n\to g$ [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on $s\setminus t$.

hypotheses.text: The functions $f_n$ and $g$ are [measurable](c:measurable-function), and $s$ is a measurable set.
The set $s$ has [finite measure](c:finite-measure): $\mu(s)<\infty$.
For $\mu$-almost every $x\in s$, $f_n(x)\to g(x)$.
The tolerance $\varepsilon$ is positive.

conclusion: There is a measurable $t\subseteq s$ with $\mu(t)\le\varepsilon$ such that $f_n\to g$ uniformly on $s\setminus t$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes strongly measurable functions into a pseudo-extended-metric space, any countable directed index set, and $\varepsilon$ in $[0,\infty]$ with $\varepsilon>0$. The statement here takes real-valued functions indexed by $\mathbb N$.

proofs.name: Shrinking bad sets
proofs.slogan: Cut out, for each tolerance $1/k$, a set of measure below $\varepsilon/2^k$ beyond which the functions stay within $1/k$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for real-valued functions on a set of finite measure. The null set where convergence fails is absorbed because it lies inside every bad set from some index on.

roles.why: Measurability makes the bad sets measurable, so their measures are defined.
Finite measure lets measures of decreasing sets converge to the measure of their intersection.
Almost everywhere convergence makes the intersection of the bad sets null.
A positive tolerance allows the bounds $\varepsilon/2^k$ and a small total measure.

steps.slogan: Define the bad sets $E(k,N)$ where some later term is $1/k$ away from $g$.
steps.detail: For $k,N\ge1$ let $E(k,N)=\{x\in s:\ |f_n(x)-g(x)|>1/k\text{ for some }n\ge N\}$. It is a countable union of [measurable](c:measurable-function) sets, so it is measurable, and it decreases as $N$ grows.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mu(E(k,N))\to0$ as $N\to\infty$ for each $k$.
steps.detail: A point of $\bigcap_NE(k,N)$ has $f_n(x)\not\to g(x)$, so $\bigcap_NE(k,N)$ lies in a null set. Since $\mu(s)<\infty$, the measures of the decreasing sets $E(k,N)$ converge to the measure of their intersection, which is $0$. This uses [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere) convergence and [finite measure](c:finite-measure).

steps.slogan: Choose an index $N_k$ with $\mu(E(k,N_k))<\varepsilon/2^k$ for each $k$.
steps.detail: By the previous step, for each $k$ some $N_k$ gives $\mu(E(k,N_k))<\varepsilon/2^k$ because $\varepsilon/2^k>0$.

steps.slogan: Take the union $t$ of the sets $E(k,N_k)$ and bound its measure.
steps.detail: Let $t=\bigcup_kE(k,N_k)$. It is a measurable subset of $s$, and $\mu(t)\le\sum_k\varepsilon/2^k=\varepsilon$ by countable subadditivity.

steps.slogan: Show that the functions converge [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on $s\setminus t$.
steps.detail: Let $x\in s\setminus t$ and $k\ge1$. Then $x\notin E(k,N_k)$, so $|f_n(x)-g(x)|\le1/k$ for every $n\ge N_k$. The index $N_k$ does not depend on $x$, which is uniform convergence on $s\setminus t$.

concepts.c:finite-measure: Finite measure lets decreasing sets lose measure in the limit.
concepts.c:measurable-function: Measurability of the functions makes the bad sets measurable.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: Pointwise convergence off a null set makes the bad sets shrink to a null set.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: The conclusion is uniform convergence off a small set.

source.note: mathlib defines notConvergentSeq, shows its measure tends to zero (measure_notConvergentSeq_tendsto_zero), picks indices (notConvergentSeqLTIndex) and takes iUnionNotConvergentSeq of measure at most epsilon.

statement: Let $f\colon M\to N$ be a surjective [submersion](c:submersion) between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) that is a [proper map](c:proper-map). Then $f$ is a locally trivial [fibre bundle](c:fibre-bundle).

hypotheses.text: $M$ and $N$ are [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold), Hausdorff and second countable, and $f\colon M\to N$ is smooth.
The map $f$ is a [submersion](c:submersion): $df$ is surjective at every point.
The map $f$ is [proper](c:proper-map): preimages of compact sets are compact.
The map $f$ is surjective.

conclusion: Every point of $N$ has an open neighborhood $U$ and a diffeomorphism $f^{-1}(U)\to U\times F$ that commutes with the projections to $U$.

proofs.name: Lifted coordinate flows
proofs.slogan: Lift the coordinate vector fields of a chart of $N$ to $M$ and compose their flows to trivialize $f$ over the chart.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the argument is local on $N$. Surjectivity is not used: over a point with empty fibre it gives $F=\emptyset$.

roles.why: Smooth manifolds give charts, partitions of unity and smooth flows.
Surjectivity of $df$ gives local lifts of vector fields and makes the fibre a submanifold.
Compact preimages keep the integral curves of the lifted fields inside $M$.
The construction is local on $N$ and also works over points with empty fibre.

steps.slogan: Fix $y_0\in N$ and a chart that sends a neighborhood $B$ of $y_0$ onto a cube.
steps.detail: Choose a chart of $N$ that sends $y_0$ to $0$ and a neighborhood $B$ onto $(-1,1)^n$, with coordinates $y_1,\dots,y_n$. Since $f$ is a submersion, $0$ is a [regular value](c:regular-value), so $F=f^{-1}(y_0)$ is a submanifold of $M$. It is compact because $f$ is proper.

steps.slogan: Lift each coordinate field $\partial/\partial y_i$ to a smooth vector field $\xi_i$ on $f^{-1}(B)$.
steps.detail: Near each point of $f^{-1}(B)$, a submersion has the form $(x,y)\mapsto y$ in suitable coordinates, so $\partial/\partial y_i$ lifts there. The condition $df(\xi)=\partial/\partial y_i$ is affine, so a [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) glues the local lifts into one smooth field $\xi_i$ with $df(\xi_i)=\partial/\partial y_i$.

steps.slogan: Show that the flows of the lifted fields exist for all times that keep the base inside $B$.
steps.detail: An integral curve of $\xi_i$ lies over an integral line of $\partial/\partial y_i$. While that line stays in $B$, the curve stays in the preimage of a compact segment, which is compact because $f$ is proper, so the curve cannot escape. Hence the [flow](c:flow-of-a-vector-field) $\varphi^i_t$ is defined, smooth in $(t,x)$, and satisfies $f(\varphi^i_t(x))=f(x)+te_i$.

steps.slogan: Compose the flows to build a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) $F\times B\to f^{-1}(B)$ over $B$.
steps.detail: Define $\Phi(x,y)=\varphi^1_{y_1}\circ\cdots\circ\varphi^n_{y_n}(x)$; each partial composition stays over the cube, so $\Phi$ is defined and $f(\Phi(x,y))=y$. The map $\Psi(z)=(\varphi^n_{-y_n}\circ\cdots\circ\varphi^1_{-y_1}(z),\,y)$ with $y=f(z)$ is smooth, lands in $F\times B$, and inverts $\Phi$ because flows compose as a group. So $\Phi$ trivializes $f$ over $B$.

concepts.c:submersion: Submersion lets coordinate fields of the base lift to the total space.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Charts, partitions of unity and flows need smooth manifolds.
concepts.c:proper-map: Properness keeps lifted integral curves from escaping to infinity.
concepts.c:fibre-bundle: The conclusion is local triviality of the map as a fibre bundle.
concepts.c:regular-value: A regular value has a fibre that is a submanifold.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: A partition of unity glues the local lifts of a vector field.
concepts.c:flow-of-a-vector-field: The flows of the lifted fields move points between fibres.
concepts.c:diffeomorph: The composed flows give a diffeomorphism from the product onto the preimage.

source.note: The standard proof by lifting coordinate vector fields and integrating them; the theorem is Voisin, Hodge Theory and Complex Algebraic Geometry I, Theorem 9.3.

statement: Let $a$ be an [irrational number](c:irrational-number). For all $0\le c<d\le1$, $\frac1N\#\{1\le n\le N:\{na\}\in[c,d)\}\to d-c$ as $N\to\infty$, where $\{x\}$ is the fractional part of $x$.

hypotheses.text: The number $a$ is [irrational](c:irrational-number).

conclusion: The sequence $a,2a,3a,\dots$ is uniformly distributed modulo $1$: the frequency of the points in $[c,d)$ tends to the length $d-c$.

proofs.name: Exponential sums and approximation
proofs.slogan: Show that averages of $e^{2\pi ihna}$ vanish for $h\ne0$, extend to continuous functions by approximation, then squeeze intervals.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by Weyl's argument. Intervals touching $0$ or $1$ are handled through the periodic extension of their indicator functions.

roles.why: Irrationality gives $e^{2\pi iha}\ne1$ for every nonzero integer $h$, so the geometric sums stay bounded.

steps.slogan: Sum the [geometric series](c:geometric-series) $\sum_{n\le N}e^{2\pi ihna}$ and show that its average tends to $0$.
steps.detail:
For an integer $h
e0$, $z=e^{2\pi iha}

steps.slogan: Extend the limit to every [trigonometric polynomial](c:trigonometric-polynomial) by linearity.
steps.detail: For $P(x)=\sum_{|h|\le H}c_he^{2\pi ihx}$, the term $h=0$ is constant and the other terms average to $0$. So $\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^NP(na)\to c_0=\int_0^1P(x)\,dx$.

steps.slogan: Approximate a continuous periodic function by trigonometric polynomials to pass the limit to it.
steps.detail: Let $f$ be continuous with period $1$ and let $\varepsilon>0$. By the Weierstrass approximation theorem, some trigonometric polynomial $P$ satisfies $\sup|f-P|<\varepsilon$, a [uniform](c:uniform-convergence) approximation, so the averages of $f$ and of $P$ along $na$ differ by less than $\varepsilon$, and so do $\int_0^1f$ and $\int_0^1P$. Hence the $\limsup$ of $\left|\frac1N\sum_{n\le N}f(na)-\int_0^1f\right|$ is at most $2\varepsilon$, so it is $0$.

steps.slogan: Squeeze the indicator of $[c,d)$ between continuous periodic functions of nearly equal integral.
steps.detail: For $\varepsilon>0$ choose continuous periodic $f_-\le\mathbf 1_{[c,d)}\le f_+$ with $\int_0^1f_+\le d-c+\varepsilon$ and $\int_0^1f_-\ge d-c-\varepsilon$. Averaging along $na$ bounds the frequency $\frac1N\#\{n\le N:\{na\}\in[c,d)\}$ between the averages of $f_-$ and $f_+$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon$ tend to $0$ to get the limit $d-c$ of the frequency.
steps.detail: By the previous steps, the $\liminf$ of the frequency is at least $d-c-\varepsilon$ and its $\limsup$ is at most $d-c+\varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, the frequency tends to $d-c$.

concepts.c:irrational-number: Irrationality keeps the exponential sums bounded for every nonzero frequency.
concepts.c:geometric-series: Each exponential sum is a geometric series with closed form.
concepts.c:trigonometric-polynomial: Finite exponential sums are the functions for which the limit is computed.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform approximation transfers the limit from polynomials to continuous functions.

source.note: Weyl's argument, from H. Weyl, Über die Gleichverteilung von Zahlen mod. Eins, Math. Ann. 77 (1916), 313-352.

statement: Let $X$ be a compact metric space, $T\colon X\to X$ continuous, and $\mu$ a $T$-[invariant measure](c:invariant-measure) (a Borel probability measure). Then there is a Borel probability measure $\tau$ on the set of [ergodic measures](c:ergodic-measure) with $\mu(B)=\int\nu(B)\,d\tau(\nu)$ for every Borel set $B$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a compact metric space and $T\colon X\to X$ is continuous.
$\mu$ is a Borel probability measure with $\mu(T^{-1}B)=\mu(B)$ for every Borel set $B$.

conclusion: The measure $\mu$ is a mixture of ergodic invariant probability measures: $\mu=\int\nu\,d\tau(\nu)$ for a probability measure $\tau$ on the ergodic measures.

proofs.name: Choquet's theorem on the invariant measures
proofs.slogan: The invariant measures form a compact convex set whose extreme points are the ergodic measures, and Choquet's theorem decomposes $\mu$ over them.
proofs.scope: Compact metric spaces with a continuous map; the uniqueness of $\tau$ is not proved here. A Borel set $A$ is invariant if $T^{-1}A=A$, and an invariant measure is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or $1$.

roles.why: Compactness and continuity make the invariant measures a compact convex metrizable set.
The given measure $\mu$ lies in the compact convex set that Choquet's theorem decomposes.

steps.slogan: Show that the invariant probability measures form a compact convex metrizable set $\mathcal M$.
steps.detail: By the Riesz-Markov-Kakutani theorem the Borel probability measures form a closed subset of the unit ball of $C(X)^*$ in the [weak-star topology](c:weak-star-topology), which is compact and metrizable because $C(X)$ is separable. The condition $\int f\circ T\,d\nu=\int f\,d\nu$ for all $f\in C(X)$ is weak-star closed and [convex](c:convex-set) because $T$ is continuous.

steps.detail: The two previous steps show that the extreme points of $\mathcal M$ are exactly the ergodic measures, and they form a $G_\delta$ set because $\mathcal M$ is metrizable. concepts.c:invariant-measure: The invariant measures are the points of the compact convex set.
concepts.c:ergodic-measure: The ergodic measures are exactly the extreme points of that set.
concepts.c:extreme-point: Choquet's theorem decomposes a point over the extreme points.
concepts.c:convex-set: Invariance is preserved by convex combinations, so the set is convex.
concepts.c:weak-star-topology: The weak-star topology makes the set of invariant measures compact.

source.note: The Choquet-theoretic proof: see R. R. Phelps, Lectures on Choquet's Theorem, 2nd edition, Springer LNM 1757 (2001), and P. Walters, An Introduction to Ergodic Theory, Springer GTM 79 (1982), for the ergodic measures as extreme points.

statement: Let $R$ be a real $3\times3$ [rotation matrix](c:rotation-matrix), that is, $R^{\mathsf T}R=I$ and $\det R=1$. Then $R$ fixes a unit vector $u$, and in an orthonormal basis $(u,v,w)$ it rotates the plane spanned by $v,w$ by some angle. Hence the composition of two rotations is a rotation about some axis.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $R$ satisfies $R^{\mathsf T}R=I$, so it preserves inner products.
The [determinant](c:determinant) of $R$ is $1$.

conclusion: There are a unit vector $u$ with $Ru=u$ and an angle $\theta$ such that, in an orthonormal basis $(u,v,w)$, $R$ has the block form $1\oplus\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$.

proofs.name: Determinant and fixed axis
proofs.slogan: Show that $\det(R-I)=0$, take a fixed unit vector as the axis, and read $R$ on the orthogonal plane.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A rigid displacement of space that fixes a point is an orthogonal map of determinant $1$, which models the geometric statement.

roles.why: Orthogonality gives $RR^{\mathsf T}=I$ and makes $R$ preserve the plane orthogonal to the axis.
Determinant $1$ makes $\det(R-I)$ equal to its own negative and fixes the block determinant.

steps.slogan: Show that $\det(R-I)=0$ by comparing it with $\det(I-R)$.
steps.detail: Since $RR^{\mathsf T}=I$ and $\det R=1$, $\det(R-I)=\det\big(R(I-R^{\mathsf T})\big)=\det R\cdot\det\big((I-R)^{\mathsf T}\big)=\det(I-R)$. For a $3\times3$ matrix $\det(I-R)=-\det(R-I)$. So $\det(R-I)=-\det(R-I)$, which gives $0$.

steps.slogan: Take a unit vector $u$ in the kernel of $R-I$ as the axis.
steps.detail: Because $\det(R-I)=0$, the matrix $R-I$ has a nonzero kernel vector, so $1$ is an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) of $R$. Scale a kernel vector to length $1$ to get $u$ with $Ru=u$.

steps.slogan: Show that $R$ maps the plane orthogonal to $u$ into itself.
steps.detail: Let $x\perp u$. Since $R$ preserves inner products, $\langle Rx,u\rangle=\langle Rx,Ru\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle=0$. So $R$ maps $u^\perp$ into itself, and bijectively because $R$ is invertible.

steps.slogan: Write $R$ in an orthonormal basis adapted to $u$ and isolate the block on $u^\perp$.
steps.detail: Choose an orthonormal basis $(u,v,w)$ with $v,w\in u^\perp$. Then $R=1\oplus Q$ for a $2\times2$ matrix $Q$ with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I$ and $\det Q=\det R=1$.

steps.slogan: Identify an orthogonal $2\times2$ matrix of determinant $1$ as a rotation by an angle $\theta$.
steps.detail: The first column of $Q$ is a unit vector $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. The second column is a unit vector orthogonal to it, so it is $\pm(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$, and $\det Q=1$ selects the sign $+$. So $Q$ is the rotation by $\theta$, and $R$ rotates about the axis $u$ by $\theta$.

concepts.c:rotation-matrix: The theorem describes the geometry of every rotation matrix.
concepts.c:determinant: The determinant identity forces the eigenvalue $1$ in odd dimension.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The eigenvalue $1$ gives the fixed axis of the rotation.

source.note: The classical determinant argument in linear algebra; mathlib has no Euler rotation theorem.

statement: Let $E$ be a separable [Banach space](c:banach-space) and $\mu$ a [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) on $E$. Then there is $C>0$ such that $\int e^{C\|x\|^2}\,d\mu(x)<\infty$.

hypotheses.text: $E$ is a separable [Banach space](c:banach-space) with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
$\mu$ is a [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure): a Borel probability measure whose image under every continuous linear functional is a normal law.

conclusion: For some $C>0$ the function $x\mapsto e^{C\|x\|^2}$ is [integrable](c:integrability) with respect to $\mu$.

proofs.name: Rotation invariance of the symmetrization
proofs.slogan: Symmetrize the measure, use rotation invariance to get a double-exponential tail, integrate over shells, and return to the original measure.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Degenerate normal laws are allowed, and the case where the symmetrized measure lives in a ball is trivial.

roles.why: Separability and completeness make a Borel measure on $E\times E$ determined by its characteristic functionals.
Gaussian functionals make the symmetrization centered Gaussian and give the rotation invariance.

steps.slogan: Pass to the symmetrization $\nu$, the law of $X-Y$ for independent copies $X,Y$ of $\mu$.
steps.detail: Let $\nu$ be the [convolution](c:convolution) of $\mu$ with its reflection, the image of $\mu$ under $x\mapsto-x$. For every continuous linear functional $L$, $L(X-Y)$ is a difference of independent normal variables with the same law, so it is centered normal. Hence $\nu$ is a centered Gaussian measure.

steps.slogan: Show that $\nu\otimes\nu$ is invariant under the rotation $(u,v)\mapsto((u+v)/\sqrt2,(v-u)/\sqrt2)$.
steps.detail:
Let $q(L)=\operatorname{Var}L$ under $
u$, a quadratic form on the dual. The characteristic functional of the [product measure](c:product-measure) $
u\otimes
u$ is $\exp(-	frac12(q(L_1)+q(L_2)))$, and the parallelogram law for $q$ shows that rotating $(L_1,L_2)$ leaves it unchanged. A Borel measure on the separable Banach space $E	imes E$ is determined by its characteristic functional.

steps.slogan: Choose a ball of measure above one half and derive a double-exponential tail bound for $\nu$.
steps.detail:
Pick $a>0$ with $m=
u\{\|x\|\le a\}>1/2$; if $m=1$, then $
u$ lives in a ball and any $C$ works. Rotation invariance gives $m\,
u\{\|x\|>b\}\le
u\{\|x\|>(b-a)/\sqrt2\}^2$ for $b>a$. With $t_0=a$ and $t_{n+1}=\sqrt2\,t_n+a$ this gives $
u\{\|x\|>t_n\}\le m ig((1-m)/m ig)^{2^n}$.

steps.slogan: Sum over shells to show that $e^{c\|x\|^2}$ is integrable for $\nu$ when $c>0$ is small.
steps.detail: On the shell $t_n<\|x\|\le t_{n+1}$ we have $\|x\|^2\le\kappa\,2^n$ for a constant $\kappa$ that depends only on $a$. Choose $c>0$ with $c\kappa<\tfrac12\log\frac m{1-m}$. Then the shell contributes at most $m\exp(-\tfrac12\log\tfrac m{1-m}\,2^n)$, a summable series, and the ball $\|x\|\le a$ contributes at most $e^{ca^2}$.

steps.slogan: Transfer integrability from $\nu$ back to $\mu$ with Tonelli's theorem and a norm inequality.
steps.detail: By Tonelli, $\iint e^{c\|x-y\|^2}\,d\mu(x)\,d\mu(y)=\int e^{c\|z\|^2}\,d\nu(z)<\infty$, so some $y$ has $\int e^{c\|x-y\|^2}\,d\mu(x)<\infty$. Since $\|x\|^2\le2\|x-y\|^2+2\|y\|^2$, we get $e^{(c/2)\|x\|^2}\le e^{c\|y\|^2}e^{c\|x-y\|^2}$, which is $\mu$-integrable. So $C=c/2$ works.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness and separability support the measure theory on $E$ and $E\times E$.
concepts.c:gaussian-measure: Gaussian functionals make the symmetrization centered Gaussian and rotation invariant.
concepts.c:integrability: The conclusion is integrability of $e^{C\|x\|^2}$ with respect to $\mu$.
concepts.c:convolution: The symmetrization is the convolution of $\mu$ with its reflection.
concepts.c:product-measure: The rotation invariance is a statement about the product measure $\nu\otimes\nu$.

source.note: mathlib symmetrizes mu to mu convolved with its reflection, proves rotation invariance (map_rotation_eq_self_of_forall_strongDual_eq_zero) and the tail recursion (exists_integrable_exp_sq_of_map_rotation_eq_self), then returns to mu with integrable_exp_sq_of_conv_neg.
